oil.summary: Crude markets suffered one of the sharpest single-day collapses in recent memory as the U.S.-Iran agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz drained the geopolitical war premium in one session. WTI shed 7.18% to $74.95/bbl and Brent fell 5.49% to $78.60/bbl, extending a brutal month that has now wiped roughly 28-29% off both benchmarks. The deal, expected to be formally signed in Geneva on June 19, includes an Iranian oil sanctions waiver allowing crude sales to resume immediately without waiting for inspections or certifications. Demand headwinds compounded the supply relief: Chinese refinery runs hit a four-year low as crude imports dropped to an eight-year low. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs cut year-end and 2027 price forecasts in response. Trump also flagged the possibility of reimposing Russian crude sanctions, a residual upside tail risk that traders are not yet pricing meaningfully.
drivers: U.S.-Iran Hormuz deal triggers immediate unwinding of geopolitical risk premium; Iranian barrels to re-enter market without delay
China demand destruction — refinery runs at four-year low, crude imports at eight-year low — amplifies bearish price pressure
Major bank forecast cuts (Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs) and CME options implying 77% probability of an OPEC production increase reinforce downside bias
sources: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

gas.summary: Natural gas markets are sending divergent signals across geographies. Henry Hub edged up 2.89% on the day to $3.238/MMBtu, extending a month-long grind higher of 9.39%, supported partly by a labour strike at Inpex's Australian LNG facilities that threatens to disrupt global supply chains. TTF, by contrast, dropped 1.96% to €41.675/MWh and is down 14.50% on the week, as the Hormuz deal raises expectations of a near-term Qatari LNG restart within weeks. ConocoPhillips is also reportedly set to become the first U.S. major to sign a post-war Syrian gas development deal, signalling medium-term supply additions. News flow for this sector today is moderate; the Australian strike and Qatar restart timeline are the primary near-term swing factors for LNG pricing.
drivers: Ongoing strike at Inpex Australian LNG facilities introduces near-term supply disruption, supporting Henry Hub
Qatar signalling rapid LNG output restoration post-Hormuz reopening weighs on TTF and European forward prices
ConocoPhillips Syria gas deal adds medium-term supply optionality to the regional market

power.summary: Power and carbon markets were relatively quiet on the day. EU EUAs were essentially flat at $75.56, down just 0.02%, though the contract has gained 5.06% over the past week and 5.75% over the month — a divergence from TTF's sharp slide that may reflect tightening EU policy expectations rather than fuel-switching dynamics. TTF's 14.50% weekly decline would ordinarily reduce carbon abatement incentives in gas-for-coal switching, a relationship worth monitoring. On the geopolitical side, UK PM Starmer used the G7 to announce a £210 million nuclear energy support package for Ukraine alongside fresh Russia sanctions, adding a structural nuclear signal. The Hormuz-related headlines feeding this sector are largely spillovers from the oil story. Dedicated power-market price data beyond EUAs and TTF was not provided today; commentary on power spot or capacity prices is therefore limited to available inputs.
drivers: EUAs hold firm near $75.56 despite TTF weakness, suggesting carbon pricing is being driven by policy expectations rather than near-term fuel-switching economics
UK G7 pledge of £210 million nuclear energy package for Ukraine highlights continued European nuclear investment momentum
Hormuz reopening and prospective Iranian crude return may soften energy import costs across Europe, potentially easing power generation cost pressures medium-term
